claim: Many neurons show compartmentalized activity, in which activity does not spread readily across the cell, allowing input and output to occur locally.
source: Many neurons show compartmentalized activity, in which activity does not spread readily across the cell, allowing input and output to occur locally.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuronal compartmentalization that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: APL inhibits Kenyon cells' dendrites and axons.
source: We used local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging to show that APL inhibits Kenyon cells' dendrites and axons
evidence: The abstract states this was demonstrated using local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Activity in APL is spatially localized.
source: We used local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging to show that APL inhibits Kenyon cells' dendrites and axons, and that both activity in APL and APL's inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells are spatially localized (the latter somewhat less so)
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding was demonstrated through local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging.

claim: APL's inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells is spatially localized, but somewhat less so than APL activity itself.
source: We used local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging to show that APL inhibits Kenyon cells' dendrites and axons, and that both activity in APL and APL's inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells are spatially localized (the latter somewhat less so)
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this comparative finding about the spatial extent of APL activity versus its inhibitory effect.

claim: APL can differentially inhibit different mushroom body compartments.
source: We used local stimulation and volumetric calcium imaging to show that APL inhibits Kenyon cells' dendrites and axons, and that both activity in APL and APL's inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells are spatially localized (the latter somewhat less so), allowing APL to differentially inhibit different mushroom body compartments.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the spatially localized activity and inhibition demonstrated in the experiments.

claim: Individual Kenyon cells inhibit themselves via APL more strongly than they inhibit other individual Kenyon cells.
source: Applying these results to the Drosophila hemibrain connectome predicts that individual Kenyon cells inhibit themselves via APL more strongly than they inhibit other individual Kenyon cells.
evidence: This prediction is based on applying physiological measurements to connectome data, as stated in the abstract.

claim: The Drosophila olfactory system is a numerically simple circuit.
source: These difficulties are eased in the Drosophila olfactory system, a numerically simple circuit that is now subject to intensive connectomic reconstruction (Takemura et al., 2017; Tobin et al., 2017; Scheffer et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the Drosophila olfactory system, supported by citations.

claim: The Drosophila olfactory system is subject to intensive connectomic reconstruction.
source: These difficulties are eased in the Drosophila olfactory system, a numerically simple circuit that is now subject to intensive connectomic reconstruction (Takemura et al., 2017; Tobin et al., 2017; Scheffer et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to connectomic reconstruction studies.

claim: The mushroom body is the fly's olfactory learning center.
source: We focus on the mushroom body, the fly's olfactory learning center, which has a well-characterized compartmentalized architecture (reviewed in Amin and Lin, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to a review.

claim: The mushroom body has a well-characterized compartmentalized architecture.
source: We focus on the mushroom body, the fly's olfactory learning center, which has a well-characterized compartmentalized architecture (reviewed in Amin and Lin, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to a review.

claim: Kenyon cells are the mushroom body's principal neurons.
source: The mushroom body's principal neurons, the Kenyon cells (KCs), form parallel bundles of axons that are divided into compartments by the innervation patterns of dopaminergic neurons and mushroom body output neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mushroom body anatomy.

claim: Kenyon cells form parallel bundles of axons that are divided into compartments by the innervation patterns of dopaminergic neurons and mushroom body output neurons.
source: The mushroom body's principal neurons, the Kenyon cells (KCs), form parallel bundles of axons that are divided into compartments by the innervation patterns of dopaminergic neurons and mushroom body output neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mushroom body anatomy.

claim: During olfactory associative learning, dopaminergic neurons in one compartment modify the local connection strength between Kenyon cells and mushroom body output neurons in the same compartment, but not other compartments.
source: During olfactory associative learning, dopaminergic neurons in one compartment modify the local connection strength between Kenyon cells and mushroom body output neurons in the same compartment, but not other compartments (Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on olfactory learning.

claim: The APL neuron is an inhibitory interneuron that innervates all the mushroom body compartments.
source: Superimposed on this compartmentalized structure is an inhibitory interneuron that innervates all the mushroom body compartments: the anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron (Aso et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The APL neuron ensures sparse odor coding by Kenyon cells through feedback inhibition.
source: The APL neuron ensures sparse odor coding by Kenyon cells through feedback inhibition (Lei et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APL plays a role in memory suppression and reversal learning.
source: The APL neuron ensures sparse odor coding by Kenyon cells through feedback inhibition (Lei et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014) and also plays a role in memory suppression and reversal learning (Liu and Davis, 2009; Ren et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APL is non-spiking, like its locust homolog GGN.
source: Like its locust homolog, the giant GABAergic neuron (GGN), APL is non-spiking (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The adult APL has pre- and post-synaptic specializations throughout all its processes.
source: Unlike the larval APL (Eichler et al., 2017; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2014), the adult APL has pre- and post-synaptic specializations throughout all its processes (Wu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: APL forms reciprocal synapses with Kenyon cells throughout the mushroom body.
source: connectomic reconstructions show that APL forms reciprocal synapses with Kenyon cells throughout the mushroom body (Takemura et al., 2017; Scheffer et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectomic studies.

claim: There have been reports of localized activity within APL.
source: There have been reports of localized activity within APL (Inada et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Compartmental modeling suggests that in the locust GGN, depolarization should diminish with distance from the site of current input, although not to zero.
source: compartmental modeling suggests that in the locust GGN, depolarization should diminish with distance from the site of current input, although not to zero (Ray et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: APL responds to electric shock.
source: APL responds to electric shock (Liu and Davis, 2009; Zhou et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electric shocks evoked a strong response in APL in the V region, with significantly smaller responses in the other regions.
source: Electric shocks evoked a strong response in APL in the V region, with significantly smaller responses in the other regions (Figure 1B,C, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The odor isoamyl acetate at 10−2 dilution evoked a different pattern of activity in APL than electric shock, with somewhat stronger responses in the S region and weaker in γ.
source: However, the odor isoamyl acetate at 10−2 dilution evoked a different pattern of activity, with somewhat stronger responses in the S region and weaker in γ (Figure 1B,C, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Spatially differential responses to electric shock in APL might arise from different synaptic inputs.
source: These different spatial profiles for electric shock vs. odor suggest that spatially differential responses to electric shock might arise from different synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different spatial profiles for different stimuli.

claim: APL receives more synapses from the dopaminergic neurons PPL1γ2α′1, PPL1γ1pedc and PPL1α′2α2 in the heel and stalk compared to dopaminergic neurons PPL1α3 and PPL1α′3 in the tip.
source: In support of (2), APL receives more synapses from the dopaminergic neurons PPL1γ2α′1, PPL1γ1pedc and PPL1α′2α2 in the heel and stalk, which are presumably inhibitory (Zhou et al., 2019), compared to dopaminergic neurons PPL1α3 and PPL1α′3 in the tip (Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectomic data.

claim: Voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels are expressed at lower levels in APL than in all other types of mushroom body neurons.
source: In contrast, voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels are expressed at lower levels in APL than in all other types of mushroom body neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: APL does not fire action potentials.
source: These results are consistent with previous findings that APL does not fire action potentials (Papadopoulou et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous electrophysiological study.

claim: APL must have a significant voltage-gated Ca2+ conductance despite relatively low expression of voltage-gated Ca2+ channel mRNA.
source: However, note that relative somatic mRNA expression (transcripts per million) may not necessarily translate into absolute protein abundance or ion conductance. Indeed, despite the relatively low expression of voltage-gated Ca2+ channel mRNA, APL must have a significant voltage-gated Ca2+ conductance.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental results showing that histamine application reduces Ca2+ influx in APL.

claim: When APL expresses Ort, histamine strongly reduces odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in APL.
source: Indeed, when APL expresses Ort, histamine strongly reduces odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in APL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ influx in APL is in large part voltage-dependent.
source: Indeed, when APL expresses Ort, histamine strongly reduces odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in APL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Ca2+ influx in APL is in large part voltage-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that histamine (which hyperpolarizes via Cl- conductance) reduces Ca2+ influx.

claim: Activating only the α′β′ Kenyon cells activates only the α′ lobe of APL.
source: When we activated only the α′β′ Kenyon cells using 853-GAL4 > dTRPA1 (Silies et al., 2013), remarkably, only the α′ lobe of APL responded (Figure 3A–C,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Activating only αβ/γ Kenyon cells activates only the α lobe of APL.
source: The same occurred for the α lobe when we activated only αβ/γ Kenyon cells using mb247-GAL4 > dTRPA1 (Figure 3D–F,I)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: APL neurites in the unresponsive lobe failed to respond despite being only 2–3 µm away from responding neurites.
source: APL neurites in the unresponsive lobe failed to respond despite being only 2–3 µm away from responding neurites.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described in Figure 3.

claim: APL neurites in the vertical lobe mostly run in parallel along Kenyon cells and do not cross between the α and α′ lobes.
source: This can most likely be explained by the fact that APL neurites in the vertical lobe mostly run in parallel along Kenyon cells and do not cross between the α and α′ lobes (Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to connectomic data.

claim: Local stimulation of APL with P2X2 + ATP decays to undetectable levels within as little as 100 µm.
source: In contrast, we found that local stimulation of APL with P2X2 + ATP decayed to undetectable levels within as little as 100 µm.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Local stimulation of APL evoked intense GCaMP6f responses at the site of ATP application, but not at the unstimulated site.
source: This local stimulation evoked intense GCaMP6f responses at the site of ATP application, but not at the unstimulated site (Figure 4A,D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activity in APL attenuates to undetectable levels across the breadth of the neuron (about 250–300 µm).
source: This local stimulation evoked intense GCaMP6f responses at the site of ATP application, but not at the unstimulated site (Figure 4A,D), indicating that activity in APL attenuates to undetectable levels across the breadth of the neuron (about 250–300 µm; see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that local stimulation does not activate distant sites.

claim: Stimulating Kenyon cells in the calyx evoked a strong response in APL in both the calyx and the vertical lobe.
source: In contrast to stimulating APL, stimulating Kenyon cells in the calyx evoked a strong response in APL in both the calyx and the vertical lobe (Figure 4B,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stimulating Kenyon cells at the tip of the vertical lobe activated APL locally, but not in the calyx.
source: However, stimulating Kenyon cells at the tip of the vertical lobe activated APL locally, but not in the calyx (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activity evoked by stimulation at the tip of the vertical lobe decayed to an undetectable level by the branching point between the two lobes.
source: Strikingly, activity evoked by stimulation at the tip of the vertical lobe decayed to an undetectable level by the branching point between the two lobes (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Local stimulation of APL in the lobes strongly reduced the baseline GCaMP6f signal in Kenyon cells locally, but also had a smaller widespread effect.
source: Local stimulation of APL in the lobes strongly reduced the baseline GCaMP6f signal in Kenyon cells locally, but also had a smaller widespread effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: When stimulating APL in the horizontal lobe, odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in Kenyon cells was strongly inhibited in the lower vertical lobe, but less so in the tip of the vertical lobe.
source: Strikingly, when stimulating APL in the horizontal lobe, odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in Kenyon cells was strongly inhibited in the lower vertical lobe, but less so in the tip of the vertical lobe (Figure 7A2,A4; difference between node 200 µm vs. 260 µm, p<0.01, paired t-test; see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7 with statistical analysis.

claim: APL can differentially inhibit different mushroom body compartments defined by dopaminergic and output neuron innervation.
source: That inhibition of Kenyon cell axons can differ over such a short distance suggests that APL can differentially inhibit different mushroom body compartments defined by dopaminergic and output neuron innervation (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibition differs over short distances.

claim: Puffing ATP on the calyx induced calcium influx in Kenyon cells in the calyx but inhibited calcium influx in the lobes.
source: Surprisingly, puffing ATP on the calyx induced calcium influx in Kenyon cells in the calyx but inhibited calcium influx in the lobes (Figures 6C and 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Puffing ATP on the calyx in negative control flies with UAS-P2X2 and no GAL4 induced calcium influx in Kenyon cells, but did not inhibit it anywhere.
source: This apparently puzzling result can be explained by observing that puffing ATP on the calyx in negative control flies with UAS-P2X2 and no GAL4 also induced calcium influx in Kenyon cells, but did not inhibit it anywhere (Figure 6D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sufficiently strong local inhibition in Kenyon cell dendrites can silence Kenyon cells throughout their axons.
source: These results show that sufficiently strong local inhibition in Kenyon cell dendrites can silence Kenyon cells throughout their axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of calyx stimulation effects.

claim: The inhibitory effect of APL was sometimes less localized than APL activity itself.
source: The inhibitory effect was sometimes less localized than APL activity itself.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparing APL activity and its inhibitory effects.

claim: When ATP was ejected at the tip of the vertical lobe, APL activity decreased to zero by 100 µm from the ejection site and there was no activity in the horizontal lobe.
source: For example, when ATP was ejected at the tip of the vertical lobe, APL activity decreased to zero by 100 µm from the ejection site and there was no activity in the horizontal lobe (Figures 5D,G and 7B1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: The inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells persisted into the peduncle and the horizontal lobe when ATP was ejected at the tip of the vertical lobe.
source: whereas the inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells persisted into the peduncle and the horizontal lobe (Figure 7B2), even into the calyx (>200 µm away) in the case of the inhibitory effect on Kenyon cell odor-evoked responses (Figure 7B4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Directly applying GABA caused the same inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells as locally stimulating APL with ATP.
source: In fact, directly applying GABA caused the same inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells as locally stimulating APL with ATP: strongest at the site of stimulation but still affecting them far from the site of stimulation, to a lesser extent (Figure 7, columns 3 and 5; traces in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: GABA applied to the tip of the vertical lobe inhibited Kenyon cells throughout the horizontal lobes.
source: In particular, GABA applied to the tip of the vertical lobe inhibited Kenyon cells throughout the horizontal lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the GABA application experiments.

claim: Locally inhibiting Kenyon cells in the calyx inhibited them throughout the lobes.
source: Locally inhibiting Kenyon cells in the calyx inhibited them throughout the lobes (Figure 7C3,C5, compare to Figure 7C2,C4, now without the confounding effects of leaky P2X2 expression).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: With local inhibition in the horizontal lobe, Kenyon cells were more inhibited in the lower vertical lobe than at the vertical lobe tip.
source: With local inhibition in the horizontal lobe, Kenyon cells were more inhibited in the lower vertical lobe than at the vertical lobe tip (Figure 7A3,A5, compare to Figure 7A2,A4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: All 1927 traced Kenyon cells in the hemibrain connectome form reciprocal synapses with APL in both their dendrites and axons.
source: All 1927 traced Kenyon cells in this volume form reciprocal synapses with APL (49.6 ± 17.9 APL-KC and 52.6 ± 13.4 KC-APL synapses per KC; mean ± s.d.) in both their dendrites and axons (example Kenyon cells shown in Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the hemibrain connectome dataset.

claim: APL-KC synapses are polyadic (a single presynaptic density on APL contacts multiple KCs).
source: APL-KC synapses are polyadic (a single presynaptic density on APL contacts multiple KCs).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of APL-KC synapses observed in the connectome.

claim: Each Kenyon cell inhibits itself more strongly than it inhibits other individual Kenyon cells on average.
source: In particular, each Kenyon cell inhibits itself more strongly than it inhibits other individual Kenyon cells on average (Figure 8K–M).
evidence: This is predicted by the model combining physiological measurements and connectome data, shown in Figure 8.

claim: γ, αβp and α′β′ Kenyon cells inhibit other Kenyon cells of the same subtype more than Kenyon cells of other subtypes.
source: This is due partly to the fact that γ, αβp and α′β′ Kenyon cells inhibit other Kenyon cells of the same subtype more than Kenyon cells of other subtypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Even when comparing self-inhibition to inhibition of only other Kenyon cells of the same subtype, each Kenyon cell inhibits itself more than it inhibits other individual Kenyon cells on average.
source: However, even when comparing self-inhibition to inhibition of only other Kenyon cells of the same subtype, each Kenyon cell inhibits itself more than it inhibits other individual Kenyon cells on average (Figure 8L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 8L.

claim: Activity in APL is spatially restricted for both sensory-evoked and local artificial stimulation.
source: We have shown that activity in APL is spatially restricted intracellularly for both sensory-evoked and local artificial stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Local activity in APL translates into a spatially non-uniform inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells that is strongest locally and becomes weaker farther from the site of APL stimulation.
source: This local activity in APL translates into a spatially non-uniform inhibitory effect on Kenyon cells that is strongest locally and becomes weaker farther from the site of APL stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The average Kenyon cell actually preferentially inhibits itself compared to other individual Kenyon cells.
source: Our model goes beyond these results in predicting that the average Kenyon cell actually preferentially inhibits itself (Figure 8)
evidence: This is predicted by the model combining physiological and anatomical data.

claim: A compartmental model of GGN predicts that local current injection in the α lobe should lead to depolarization throughout GGN (at least 500 µm across) though the depolarization should decrease with distance from the injection site.
source: A compartmental model of GGN predicts that local current injection in the α lobe should lead to depolarization throughout GGN (at least 500 µm across) though the depolarization should decrease with distance from the injection site (Ray et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: Activity seems to spread less far in APL than in GGN.
source: Thus, while keeping in mind the different methods used for GGN vs. APL, activity seems to spread less far in APL than in GGN.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results for APL with published results for GGN.

claim: GGN and APL have striking morphological differences.
source: In addition, although GGN and APL are both widefield inhibitory interneurons in the mushroom body, they have striking morphological differences.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing the two neurons.

claim: GGN separately innervates the lobes and calyx with numerous thin, branching processes; these tangled innervations are joined by relatively thick processes (almost 20 µm in diameter).
source: For example, GGN separately innervates the lobes and calyx with numerous thin, branching processes; these tangled innervations are joined by relatively thick processes (almost 20 µm in diameter) (Ray et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing GGN morphology.

claim: APL innervates the lobes continuously with numerous neurites that emerge in parallel from the calyx.
source: In contrast, APL innervates the lobes continuously with numerous neurites that emerge in parallel from the calyx (Mayseless et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing APL morphology.

claim: In the hemibrain connectome, APL neurites average ~0.5 µm in diameter throughout APL; ~95% of neurite length is less than 1 µm in diameter and the maximum diameter is ~3 µm.
source: In the hemibrain connectome (Scheffer et al., 2020), these neurites average ~0.5 µm in diameter throughout APL; ~95% of neurite length is less than 1 µm in diameter and the maximum diameter is ~3 µm (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the hemibrain connectome data.

claim: The larval APL has pre-synapses only in the calyx, while adult APL has pre-synapses everywhere.
source: The larval APL has pre-synapses only in the calyx, while adult APL has pre-synapses everywhere (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between larval and adult APL.

claim: The larval APL might be small enough for activity to spread passively from lobes to calyx (~100 µm) or might have different ion channel composition from adult APL.
source: The larval APL might be small enough for activity to spread passively from lobes to calyx (~100 µm) or might have different ion channel composition from adult APL.
evidence: This is speculation about possible differences between larval and adult APL.

claim: The co-ejected red dye indicator spread tens of microns from the ejection site (decay to half-strength ~10–25 µm).
source: The co-ejected red dye indicator spread tens of microns from the ejection site (decay to half-strength ~10–25 µm; see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a measurement of the spatial precision of the technique.

claim: Two-photon optogenetic stimulation has a spatial resolution of decay to half-strength 12 µm horizontal, 24 µm axially.
source: This spatial resolution is close to that of other techniques for local in vivo stimulation like two-photon optogenetic stimulation (decay to half-strength 12 µm horizontal, 24 µm axially [Packer et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ATP or GABA are likely to spread farther than the red dye, as they have lower molecular weights.
source: To the extent that ATP or GABA spread differently from the red dye, they are likely to spread farther, as they have lower molecular weights (dye: 1461; ATP: 507; GABA: 103)
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weights of the compounds.

claim: The results likely overestimate, rather than underestimate, how far APL activity and APL's inhibitory effect spread from the stimulation site.
source: meaning that our stimulation is less spatially restricted than the dye suggests. Thus, our results likely overestimate, rather than underestimate, how far APL activity and APL's inhibitory effect spread from the stimulation site.
evidence: This is inferred from the consideration that ATP/GABA likely spread farther than the dye.

claim: When puffing ATP on the horizontal or vertical lobe of KC>GCaMP6f, UAS-P2X2 control flies, Kenyon cell activity was unaffected.
source: Contrary to this prediction, when we puffed ATP on the horizontal or vertical lobe of KC>GCaMP6f, UAS-P2X2 control flies, Kenyon cell activity was unaffected (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; presumably any leaky expression of P2X2 in Kenyon cells was too low for ATP applied to their axons to excite them).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibition of Ca2+ influx in Kenyon cell axons could be stronger closer to the axon initial segment than farther from it.
source: Remarkably, inhibition of Ca2+ influx in Kenyon cell axons could be stronger closer to the axon initial segment (in the posterior peduncle [Trunova et al., 2011]) than farther from it, for example, stronger at the lower vertical lobe than the tip of the vertical lobe (Figure 7A), both when stimulating APL with ATP or when directly applying GABA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: GABA should act on Kenyon cells by suppressing depolarization through shunting inhibition in both dendrites and axons, as the GABAA receptor Rdl is expressed in both.
source: GABA should act on Kenyon cells by suppressing depolarization through shunting inhibition in both dendrites and axons, as the GABAA receptor Rdl is expressed in both (Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Local inhibition might particularly suppress Ca2+ influx rather than depolarization, perhaps by acting through GABAB receptors.
source: More likely, local inhibition might particularly suppress Ca2+ influx rather than depolarization, perhaps by acting through GABAB receptors; Kenyon cells express GABABR1 and GABABR2 (Aso et al., 2019; Crocker et al., 2016; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018) and APL inhibits KCs partly via GABAB receptors (Inada et al., 2017), although their subcellular localization is unknown.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous studies showing GABAB receptor expression and function.

claim: Kenyon cells form recurrent connections with DPM and dopaminergic neurons and form synapses and gap junctions on each other.
source: For example, Kenyon cells form recurrent connections with DPM and dopaminergic neurons and form synapses and gap junctions on each other (Liu et al., 2016; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kenyon cells indirectly excite antennal lobe neurons in a positive feedback loop.
source: Alternatively, Kenyon cells indirectly excite antennal lobe neurons in a positive feedback loop (Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some Kenyon cells can inhibit some Kenyon cells more than others.
source: This prediction is supported by previous experimental results that some Kenyon cells can inhibit some Kenyon cells more than others, and that an individual Kenyon cell can inhibit itself (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An individual Kenyon cell can inhibit itself.
source: This prediction is supported by previous experimental results that some Kenyon cells can inhibit some Kenyon cells more than others, and that an individual Kenyon cell can inhibit itself (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Blocking synaptic output from all Kenyon cells vastly increases Kenyon cell odor responses.
source: The finding of all-to-all inhibition was based on findings that whereas blocking synaptic output from all Kenyon cells vastly increases Kenyon cell odor responses (by blocking negative feedback via APL)
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' earlier work.

claim: Blocking output from one subset of Kenyon cells has no effect on (for α′β′ and γ Kenyon cells), or only weakly increases (for αβ Kenyon cells), odor responses of that subset.
source: blocking output from one subset of Kenyon cells has no effect on (for α′β′ and γ Kenyon cells), or only weakly increases (for αβ Kenyon cells), odor responses of that subset (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Local inhibition by APL would allow the single APL neuron to function effectively as multiple inhibitory interneurons.
source: This local inhibition would allow the single APL neuron to function effectively as multiple inhibitory interneurons, much like mammalian and fly amacrine cells (Grimes et al., 2010; Meier and Borst, 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of local inhibition, with citations to similar phenomena in other systems.

claim: Different compartments are innervated by different dopaminergic neurons (e.g. reward vs. punishment) and different mushroom body output neurons (e.g. avoid vs. approach).
source: Different compartments are innervated by different dopaminergic neurons (e.g. reward vs. punishment) and different mushroom body output neurons (e.g. avoid vs. approach) (Aso et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Different mushroom body compartments govern synaptic plasticity and hence learning by different rules (e.g. different speeds of learning/forgetting).
source: and they govern synaptic plasticity and hence learning by different rules (e.g. different speeds of learning/forgetting) (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Different regions of APL respond differently to dopamine.
source: Thus, APL could locally modulate different compartment-specific aspects of olfactory learning, especially given that different regions of APL respond differently to dopamine (Zhou et al., 2019) and electric shock punishment (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition from APL sparsens and decorrelates Kenyon cell odor responses to enhance learned odor discrimination.
source: Inhibition from APL sparsens and decorrelates Kenyon cell odor responses to enhance learned odor discrimination (Lin et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Decorrelation is better served by all-to-all lateral inhibition than by self-inhibition.
source: but in general, decorrelation is better served by all-to-all lateral inhibition than by self-inhibition (see Appendix 1).
